summary: This informational RFC describes a URN namespace to be used by Globus for naming persistent resources.

plainLanguage.summary: A system for giving lasting names to things Globus manages, so the names keep working.

questions: how is a globus urn structured
why does globus need a urn namespace
subtitle: A namespace for Globus to give persistent names to its resources.

tldr.problem: Globus, a research software-as-a-service provider, needed a way to create unique identifiers for its persistent resources that would be globally recognizable and would not be reassigned.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7853 defines a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace called 'globus' where Globus can create identifiers with a hierarchical structure: category identifiers (SNIDs like 'auth' for authentication) followed by optional subnamespace strings.
tldr.outcome: Globus can now use stable, unique identifiers for OAuth2 scopes, authorization grants, and entity identification across its services and third-party integrations.

today: RFC 7853 is an Internet Standard Informational RFC that defines the Globus URN namespace. It has not been obsoleted and remains the definition of how Globus creates persistent resource identifiers.

sections.title: Globus and Persistent Identifiers
sections.content:
Globus is a software-as-a-service provider that develops tools for the global research and education community, especially those using high-performance computing. As Globus operates multiple services for users across many institutions, it creates unique identifiers for resources that must persist and be identifiable as belonging to Globus. For example, when other systems reference a Globus entity, they need a way to be sure the identifier will not be reused for a different thing later.

Existing public naming systems (like the general IANA URN namespaces) were not sufficient, because Globus needed its own namespace to guarantee persistence and clarity.
sections.plainLanguage: Globus runs systems that create long-lasting names for things. It needed a system where those names would stay the same forever and everyone would know they came from Globus.

sections.title: The Globus URN Structure
sections.content:
A URN (Uniform Resource Name) is a persistent, location-independent name for a resource. The RFC defines how Globus URNs are structured: they start with the prefix urn:globus: followed by two parts. The first part is called the SNID (Subnamespace ID), a required category identifier like auth for authentication or groups for a groups service. The second part is optional and can contain more specific details, such as scope:transfer.api.globus.org:all.

This two-level hierarchy allows Globus to delegate parts of the namespace to different services while keeping the overall structure consistent. For instance, the Globus Auth service controls everything under urn:globus:auth:, while the Groups service could manage urn:globus:groups:.
sections.plainLanguage: Globus URNs follow a pattern: urn:globus:[service]:[details]. Each Globus service gets its own area (like 'auth' or 'groups'), and then can create as many specific names as it needs under that area.

sections.title: Example Globus URNs
sections.content: The RFC provides concrete examples showing how Globus services use the namespace. The Globus Auth service creates URNs for OAuth2 scopes and authorization grants, such as urn:globus:auth:scope:transfer.api.globus.org:all (a scope for the transfer API) and urn:globus:auth:grants:dependent_token (a type of authorization grant). A hypothetical Globus Groups service might create identifiers like urn:globus:groups:group:669b572e-9de4-11e5-966e-3c970e0c9cc4 for individual groups and urn:globus:groups:memberships:72e1c6c6-9de4-11e5-966e-3c970e0c9cc4 for membership records.
sections.plainLanguage: A Globus Auth URN might name a permission: 'use the transfer API'. A Globus Groups URN might name a specific group or list of members.

sections.title: Persistence and Governance
sections.content:
Once a URN is assigned, it can never be reassigned to a different resource, ensuring that any system relying on that identifier will always resolve to the same thing. The Globus Project Lead is responsible for enforcing this and managing the namespace. Globus can delegate authority over sub-parts of the namespace (specific SNIDs or subnamespace branches) to third parties, allowing partner services or organizations to safely create their own identifiers within Globus's overall structure.

Currently, there is no resolution mechanism defined (no way to look up what a URN refers to), but the RFC notes that future versions may define such resources for resolving and validating Globus identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a Globus name is assigned, it is locked in forever. Globus can let other organizations use parts of the namespace, and they are responsible for their own names.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC notes that Globus URNs have no special character meanings or encoding tricks, so there are no additional security considerations beyond those of URNs in general. There are no restrictions on the characters in the namespace-specific string beyond the standard URN syntax rules. IANA has registered globus as a formal URN namespace identifier, meaning it is officially recognized in the global registry of URN namespaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Globus URNs are straightforward and follow standard naming rules. IANA keeps an official list of URN namespaces, and 'globus' is now on it.
